### Position read
The opponent opened by moving Red from (0,3) to central square (3,3). We answered with Blue from (3,7) to the adjacent center (3,4). No losses or eliminations.

### Our plan
Contest all four central squares and aim for a split center before building capture threats. On Green’s turn, prioritize (4,3) or (4,4) if legally reachable and useful. Watch for same-color sandwich anchors; teammate colors cannot flank together.

### Opponent tendencies
The opening indicates an immediate center-occupation strategy.

### Lessons
Central occupation wins instantly, so every opponent-held center must be tracked. Moving into a sandwich is safe because captures trigger only from the mover’s landing square.

### Position read
The opponent holds (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow; we hold (3,4) with Blue. Green moved from (4,0) to (4,2), adjacent to Yellow. All colors have zero losses.

### Our plan
Blue should strongly consider occupying the empty center (4,4) next turn if legal, securing two central squares and denying it to Yellow. Green at (4,2) creates a latent sandwich against Yellow at (4,3) if a normal Green can later land on (4,4); do not mistake a Blue piece there for a valid flank. Track any opponent attempt to dislodge our Blue center piece.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent has used both opening turns to occupy central squares, signaling an aggressive center-victory plan.

### Lessons
Only matching colors form sandwich flanks. A center denial move can be valuable even when it postpones a same-color capture setup.

### Position read
The opponent holds (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow; we now contest the center with Blue at (4,4). Blue has one loss; all other colors have zero. Green remains at (4,2), separated from the center by Yellow at (4,3).

### Our plan
Prioritize center denial while developing matching-color sandwich geometry. Blue at (4,4) can be captured if Yellow moves from (7,5) to (4,5), using Yellow at (4,3) as the far flank; if that happens, note the second Blue loss and use the tempo to improve Green's position. Avoid allowing the opponent to occupy both remaining center squares in sequence.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent aggressively occupies center squares and used Red at (3,5) with Red at (3,3) to sandwich our former Blue at (3,4). Expect similarly tactical center captures.

### Lessons
Before occupying a center square, scan every legal landing beyond it for a matching-color sandwich. Forcing an opponent to capture can still be useful when it delays immediate center victory.

### Position read
The opponent occupies (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow; (3,4) and (4,4) are empty. Blue has two losses and is one capture from elimination. Green moved to (3,2), beside the Red center piece. The opponent has a direct center sequence: Red can occupy (3,4), then Yellow can move from (4,5) to (4,4).

### Our plan
If the opponent misses the center win, use Green at (3,2) as a central anchor and seek a same-color flank against Red. On Blue turns, prioritize immediate center denial and avoid any exposure because Blue's next capture eliminates it.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent aggressively takes central squares and recognizes same-color sandwich tactics. Expect Red to play (3,5) to (3,4), setting up Yellow's center completion.

### Lessons
Track two-ply center completions before committing a piece. A center occupation can be strategically losing when the opponent can sandwich it and preserve the tempo.

### Position read
The opponent holds three center squares: (3,3), (3,4), and (4,3). A Yellow piece at (4,5) can legally move to the empty (4,4), completing center occupation immediately. No current Blue move can occupy (4,4), block that horizontal move, or capture a central piece. Blue has two losses.

### Our plan
We advanced Blue from (2,7) to (2,4), the nearest useful central anchor, because the immediate center completion cannot be prevented. If play continues, prioritize breaking center control and protecting Blue from its third loss.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent executes direct center-occupation sequences and uses coordinated tempo effectively.

### Lessons
Before allowing three enemy center squares, verify whether the fourth can be occupied on the very next turn; center victory occurs instantly, leaving no reply.
